prompt:
A *graph* is a collection of points and lines (or curves), called *vertices* and *edges*, where each edge connects exactly two distinct vertices and any two vertices are connected by at most one edge. Two vertices are *adjacent* if they are connected by an edge. Graph $\mathcal G$ is *isomorphic* to $\mathcal H$ ($\mathcal G\cong\mathcal H$) if the vertices of $\mathcal G$ can be renamed with the names of the vertices of $\mathcal H$ so that both graphs have the same edges. Edge crossings in a drawing are not vertices (vertices are drawn as dots).

Which of the six figures (i)-(vi) shown are graphs? List the vertices and edges of each graph and explain why the others are not graphs.
answer: Graphs: (i) vertices A,B,C,D, edges AB, AC, AD, BD; (iii) vertices A,B,C, edges AB, BC, AC; (iv) vertices A,B,C,D,E, edges AB, AD, AE, BE, CD, CE. Not graphs: (ii) A and B are joined by two edges; (v) an edge from B ends at no vertex; (vi) E is joined to itself.

solutions.title: Check each figure against the definition
solutions.body:
- (i) Four vertices $A,B,C,D$; edges $AB,AC,AD,BD$. The crossing in the middle is not a vertex. A graph.
- (ii) $A$ and $B$ are connected twice, which the definition forbids. Not a graph.
- (iii) Vertices $A,B,C$ and edges $AB,BC,AC$ (the bent line from $A$ to $C$ is one edge). A graph.
- (iv) Vertices $A,B,C,D,E$; edges $AB,AD,AE,BE,CD,CE$. A graph.
- (v) One of the edges starting at $B$ does not end at a vertex. Not a graph.
- (vi) $E$ is connected to itself (a loop), so an edge does not join two distinct vertices. Not a graph.

**Answer: (i), (iii), (iv) are graphs; (ii), (v), (vi) are not.**

prompt:
A graph is *planar* if it is isomorphic to a graph that has been drawn in the plane without edge crossings. When a planar graph is drawn in the plane without edge crossings, it cuts the plane into regions called *faces* (the exterior region counts as a face).

*Euler's formula*: a connected planar graph with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges and $f$ faces satisfies $v-e+f=2$ (you may use this).

Prove that if $\mathcal G$ is planar and connected with $v\ge3$, then $\tfrac32f\le e\le3v-6$.
answer: Count face-edge incidences: $3f\le2e$; then Euler's formula gives $e\le3v-6$.

solutions.title: Count edges around faces
solutions.body:
**Left inequality.** If $f=1$ the graph has no cycle, so it is a tree and $e=v-1\ge2$, hence $3f=3\le4\le2e$. If $f\ge2$, every face is bounded by at least $3$ edges (the boundary of a face contains a cycle, and a cycle in a graph without loops or multiple edges has at least $3$ edges). Add up, over all faces, the number of boundary edges: this is at least $3f$. Each edge borders at most two faces, so the sum is at most $2e$. Thus $3f\le2e$, i.e. $\frac32f\le e$.

**Right inequality.** From $f\le\frac23e$ and Euler's formula, $2=v-e+f\le v-e+\frac23e=v-\frac e3$. Hence $e\le3v-6$. ∎

prompt:
The *chromatic number* $\chi$ of a graph is the smallest number of colors with which its vertices can be colored so that adjacent vertices get different colors.

Given a graph $\mathcal G$ with $v$ vertices, let $\bar\chi$ be the chromatic number of the graph obtained by taking the vertices of $\mathcal G$ and drawing edges only between those that are *not* adjacent in $\mathcal G$. Prove that $\chi+\bar\chi\ge2\sqrt v$.
answer: Each color class of $\mathcal G$ is a clique in the complement, so $\chi\bar\chi\ge v$; then AM-GM.

solutions.title: Color classes and AM-GM
solutions.body:
Color $\mathcal G$ with $\chi$ colors and let $v_i$ be the number of vertices of color $i$. Vertices of the same color are pairwise non-adjacent in $\mathcal G$, so they are pairwise adjacent in the complementary graph, and therefore need $v_i$ different colors there. Hence $\bar\chi\ge v_i$ for every $i$. Summing over the $\chi$ colors, $\chi\bar\chi\ge v_1+\cdots+v_\chi=v$.

By AM-GM, $\chi+\bar\chi\ge2\sqrt{\chi\bar\chi}\ge2\sqrt v$. ∎

prompt:
The *chromatic number* $\chi$ of a graph is the smallest number of colors with which its vertices can be colored so that adjacent vertices get different colors.

Let $\mathcal G$ be a planar graph with $\chi>5$ that has a vertex $V$ of degree at most $5$. Prove that removing $V$ (and all edges at $V$) gives a graph with fewer vertices which also has $\chi>5$. You may use the Jordan Curve Theorem: a closed loop that does not intersect itself divides the plane into an inside and an outside, and a continuous curve joining a point inside to one outside must cross the loop.
answer: If $\mathcal G-V$ were 5-colorable, recolor along two-colored chains (Kempe chains) until the neighbours of $V$ use at most 4 colors; then $V$ can be colored too.

solutions.title: Kempe chains
solutions.body:
Suppose, for contradiction, that $\mathcal G-V$ can be colored with $5$ colors. Fix such a coloring and draw $\mathcal G$ in the plane without crossings.

If the neighbours of $V$ use at most $4$ colors (in particular if $\deg V\le4$), give $V$ the unused color: $\mathcal G$ would be $5$-colorable, a contradiction. So $\deg V=5$ and its neighbours $N_1,\dots,N_5$, in clockwise order around $V$, have the five different colors $1,2,3,4,5$.

*Chain $1$-$3$.* Consider the vertices of $\mathcal G-V$ colored $1$ or $3$. If $N_1$ and $N_3$ are not joined by a walk of such vertices, take the set of all vertices reachable from $N_3$ through vertices colored $1$ or $3$ and swap the colors $1\leftrightarrow3$ on it. The coloring stays proper (vertices of the set only touch outside vertices of other colors, and no outside vertex has color $1$ or $3$ adjacent to the set), $N_3$ becomes $1$, $N_1$ keeps color $1$, so color $3$ is free at $V$, a contradiction. Hence there is a walk $W$ from $N_1$ to $N_3$ through vertices colored $1$ or $3$.

*Chain $2$-$4$.* The walk $W$ together with the edges $VN_1$ and $VN_3$ forms a closed loop through $V$ (take a path inside $W$ if it repeats vertices). By the Jordan Curve Theorem it has an inside and an outside. In the cyclic order, $N_2$ lies between $N_1$ and $N_3$ on one side, while $N_4$ and $N_5$ lie on the other, so the edges $VN_2$ and $VN_4$ leave $V$ into different regions, and $N_2,N_4$ are on opposite sides of the loop. A walk from $N_2$ to $N_4$ through vertices colored $2$ or $4$ would have to cross the loop; since the drawing has no crossings it would have to pass through a vertex of the loop, but those have colors $1$ or $3$ (or are $V$, which is not in $\mathcal G-V$). So no such walk exists. Swap $2\leftrightarrow4$ on all vertices reachable from $N_2$ through vertices colored $2$ or $4$: the coloring remains proper, $N_2$ becomes $4$, $N_4$ stays $4$, and color $2$ is free at $V$. Then $V$ can be colored $2$ and $\mathcal G$ is $5$-colorable, a contradiction.

Therefore $\mathcal G-V$ cannot be $5$-colored, i.e. it also has $\chi>5$ and has fewer vertices. ∎

prompt:
The *chromatic number* $\chi$ of a graph is the smallest number of colors with which its vertices can be colored so that adjacent vertices get different colors.

Prove the Five Color Theorem: every planar graph has $\chi\le5$. (You may use that every planar graph has a vertex of degree at most $5$, and that if a planar graph $\mathcal G$ with $\chi>5$ has a vertex of degree at most $5$, then deleting that vertex leaves a planar graph with fewer vertices that also has $\chi>5$.)
answer: A counterexample with fewest vertices would produce a smaller one by deleting a vertex of degree $\le5$.

solutions.title: Minimal counterexample
solutions.body: Suppose some planar graph has $\chi>5$ and choose one with the fewest vertices. It has a vertex of degree at most $5$, and deleting it gives a planar graph with fewer vertices and still $\chi>5$ (a subgraph of a planar graph is planar), contradicting minimality. (Equivalently, repeat the deletion; the vertex count decreases each time, and a graph with at most $5$ vertices needs at most $5$ colors, a contradiction.) Hence every planar graph has $\chi\le5$. ∎
